segments.t: This is Call My Agent, set in a Paris talent agency. Gabriel has forgotten to post an important letter. Sending this letter could help the firm through a tax audit. His colleagues Andrea and Mathias ask what happened, while a client waits outside. Listen to the French story first; you do not need to catch every word.
Cécile! Oui, super. Rappelle-moi. Salut.
Le contrôle fiscal. Cette lettre pour monsieur Jarron?
Oui, je l'ai envoyée.
J'ai pris la lettre. Je l'ai mise dans une enveloppe.
Oh non!
Je suis désolé.
À quoi ça sert de payer une assistante?
Non, Gabriel, on ne peut pas toujours tout arranger!
On a eu un appel ce matin.
Le dossier est dans un autre service.
Jarron était notre seul allié.
Il faut peut-être mettre nos comptes en ordre.
La vie, c'est une grande blague pour toi?
Tu es aussi stupide que ça?
Fais-lui un café.
Let's follow the forgotten letter. First Gabriel finishes a cheerful call, before Andrea brings up the tax audit.
Cécile! Oui, super. Rappelle-moi. Salut.

Gabriel greets his client and gives an enthusiastic yes, saying that things sound great. He asks her to call back and finishes with a casual goodbye. The request to call back is a familiar command. A hyphen joins the command to a short object word identifying the person asking for the return call.
Le contrôle fiscal.
'The tax audit.' Literally 'the fiscal control'. The describing word follows the thing being checked: the agency's tax affairs.
Cette lettre pour monsieur Jarron?
'That letter for Mr Jarron?' The first word means 'this' or 'that' in a feminine form, because the word for letter is feminine.
Oui, je l'ai envoyée.

'Yes, I sent it.' The object word refers back to the letter and comes before the helping word. It loses its vowel before the next word. Because the letter is feminine, the completed action has an additional feminine ending in writing.
J'ai pris la lettre.
'I took the letter.' The completed action uses 'have' and the past form of 'take'. Gabriel tries to remember the steps he followed.
Je l'ai mise dans une enveloppe.
'I put it in an envelope.' The object word again refers to the letter. Its feminine gender gives the completed action an extra ending in writing.
Oh non!
'Oh no!' This short reaction replaces a swearword in the episode. Gabriel suddenly realises that putting the letter in an envelope was not the same as posting it.
Je suis désolé.
'I'm sorry.' This written apology has a masculine ending because Gabriel is speaking. An apology by a woman would add a silent e.
À quoi ça sert de payer une assistante?
'What's the point of paying an assistant?' Literally 'to what does it serve to pay an assistant'. Gabriel tries to shift the blame for his own mistake.
Non, Gabriel, on ne peut pas toujours tout arranger!

'No, Gabriel, you can't always fix everything!' The short word before the action can refer to a group including the speaker, or to people in general. Here Mathias is talking about people in general as he rejects Gabriel's easy reassurance.
On a eu un appel ce matin.
'We had a call this morning.' To describe the call as a finished event, French uses a helping verb in the present followed by a participle. The last two words identify this morning.
Le dossier est dans un autre service.
'The file is in another department.' The word for 'another' follows an indefinite article. Their tax case has moved away from the person who could help them.
Jarron était notre seul allié.
'Jarron was our only ally.' The past form of 'be' describes how things stood. The word for 'only' comes before the person described: their ally.
Il faut peut-être mettre nos comptes en ordre.
'Maybe we need to put our books in order.' The first two words express necessity. Gabriel suggests doing what the audit demands, which is not what his colleagues want to hear.
La vie, c'est une grande blague pour toi?
'Is life a big joke to you?' The word for 'you' after 'for' is the full form that can stand alone. Mathias turns the problem into a personal accusation.
Tu es aussi stupide que ça?
'Are you really that stupid?' Literally 'are you as stupid as that?'. The two comparison words surround the description. Just then Herve announces Laura's arrival.
Fais-lui un café.
'Make her a coffee.' This instruction attaches 'to her' after 'make' with a hyphen. Gabriel is keen to leave the meeting and see his waiting client. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Cécile! Oui, super. Rappelle-moi. Salut.
Le contrôle fiscal. Cette lettre pour monsieur Jarron?
Oui, je l'ai envoyée.
J'ai pris la lettre. Je l'ai mise dans une enveloppe.
Oh non!
Je suis désolé.
À quoi ça sert de payer une assistante?
Non, Gabriel, on ne peut pas toujours tout arranger!
On a eu un appel ce matin.
Le dossier est dans un autre service.
Jarron était notre seul allié.
Il faut peut-être mettre nos comptes en ordre.
La vie, c'est une grande blague pour toi?
Tu es aussi stupide que ça?
Fais-lui un café.
Gabriel's missing letter has cost the agency an important ally at the tax office. You have heard how to describe completed actions, apologise and ask what happened. See you next time!
À bientôt!
